overview: Two atlas records call enormous and changing parts of Mesoamerica “Maize farmers.” That is a subsistence shortcut, not the name of one people. From 1500 to 323 BCE, one polygon first stretches from western and central Mexico through much of Central America; by 400 BCE the same id is split into two features as Zapotec and Olmec areas receive separate labels. After an unexplained 123-year map gap, a smaller 200 to 100 BCE polygon wraps around regions labeled Teotihuacan, Monte Alban, and Maya. Archaeology reveals many local histories instead: lakeside villages, forest gardens, dry-valley fields, reservoirs, fisheries, pottery traditions, obsidian networks, public plazas, growing towns, and households with unequal access to labor and goods. Maize mattered deeply, yet people also cultivated beans, squash, chili, manioc, cacao, and tree foods while hunting, fishing, and gathering. Pots, plant remains, grinding stones, bones, isotope ratios, houses, burials, canals, monuments, and radiocarbon dates answer different questions. They do not reveal a shared language, government, family system, or identity across the color. This card follows connected experiments in food, community, craft, water, and power while keeping every community distinct.

periods.title: 1500 to 1200 BCE: the broad label begins
periods.summary: The atlas replaces an even larger earlier umbrella with one “Maize farmers” polygon while mapping Olmec and other neighbors separately. Across the painted zone, some communities already occupied permanent villages, made pottery, farmed, fished, and exchanged goods. Timing and combinations varied, so 1500 BCE is a software boundary rather than a coordinated agricultural beginning.

periods.title: 1200 to 900 BCE: villages connect without becoming one culture
periods.summary: Lakeside Tlatilco, Oaxacan settlements, northern Honduran villages, Maya lowland communities, and many poorly preserved places followed different paths. Cacao residue, pottery, obsidian, figurines, and food remains show movement and local invention. Similar objects can record exchange or imitation; they do not automatically identify migrants, language, political control, or shared ethnicity.

periods.title: 900 to 700 BCE: labor reshapes fields, water, and exchange
periods.summary: The broad atlas geometry remains unchanged, but evidence grows more regionally detailed. Communities built reservoirs and catchments, expanded obsidian networks, and developed local ceramic sequences. These projects required planning and cooperation, sometimes unequal leadership. They did not require a single Mesoamerican authority, one farming method, or one calendar shared identically everywhere.

periods.title: 700 to 500 BCE: public places and sharper differences
periods.summary: Household deposits, public plazas, specialist crafts, monuments, and larger settlements reveal changing social relationships. Proposed early writing appears only in specific contexts and remains debated. The atlas still paints most sampled places one color, even while archaeology distinguishes Oaxacan, Maya, Gulf Coast, central Mexican, western, and southeastern traditions.

periods.title: 500 to 400 BCE: named centers expose the umbrella
periods.summary: Monte Alban begins on an Oaxacan hilltop around 500 BCE, while Cuicuilco and other centers grow in central Mexico and Maya settlements develop along separate trajectories. The atlas retains one broad target feature through the 500 BCE snapshot. Monumental building and hierarchy expanded unevenly; rural households and smaller communities remained essential.

periods.title: 400 to 323 BCE: one id becomes two map pieces
periods.summary: The 400 BCE file contains two distinct polygons with the same target id and interval, not two documented “Maize farmer” peoples. Zapotec and Olmec features occupy separate map spaces between them. At 323 BCE both target pieces vanish. This is a database and legend transition, not evidence of conquest, migration, crop failure, or extinction.

periods.title: 323 to 200 BCE: an editorial gap full of history
periods.summary: Neither exact target id appears at 323 or 300 BCE, although farming communities, centers, exchange, water management, and writing experiments continue. A securely dated San Bartolo day sign falls within this gap, which makes its exclusion especially clear. The 123-year blank belongs to atlas classification, not to ancient population or agriculture.

periods.title: 200 to 100 BCE: a smaller residual farming label
periods.summary: The second id appears once as a polygon with three rings beside separately mapped Teotihuacan, Monte Alban, and Maya areas. It still covers diverse central and Gulf Mexican communities, not one polity. Teotihuacan begins rapid growth near the interval’s end; the target disappears at 100 BCE while people, crops, settlements, and routes continue.

sections.title: Read the atlas label before believing it

items.text: The index contains exactly two culture records named “Maize farmers”: 1500 to 323 BCE and 200 to 100 BCE. Neither had a card, summary, or override. Their matching name supports one comparative card, but it supplies no ancient self-name, language, ancestry, government, territory, or proof of continuous membership.

All fifty border snapshots were audited. The first id occurs in five files, but there are six features because world-bc400 contains two separate polygons with the same id and interval. Coverage correctly lists five files and five unique intervals while hiding that duplicate geometry, a useful software fact rather than a historical discovery.

From 1500 through 500 BCE, the target uses one identical 339-position polygon spanning roughly 111 degrees west to 78 degrees west. It includes sampled points from western Mexico through Panama while excluding separate Olmec and neighboring regions. A smooth outline cannot make those communities economically, politically, or culturally smooth.

At 400 BCE, two target polygons divide northern-central Mexico from southeastern Mexico and Central America. At 200 BCE, a different 126-position polygon has three rings and shares arcs with Teotihuacan, Monte Alban, Maya, and desert hunter-gatherer features. Shared topology records tiling, not agreed ancient frontiers.

The first color stops at 323 BCE, and the second begins at 200 BCE. Maize cultivation does not take a 123-year vacation because a map key does. Sharing one card lets the gap and label reuse stay visible, while separate overrides preserve each exact interval and leave both “falls” safely null.

sections.title: Grow food in many landscapes, not one giant field

items.text: Early and Middle Preclassic Maya plant evidence combines maize, manioc, chili peppers, gathered fruits, and other wild foods. Canals and terraces appear unevenly as village life becomes archaeologically clearer. Preservation favors charred seeds, starch, pollen, and phytoliths differently, so a missing bean is not proof that nobody cooked beans.

At Altica, macro- and microbotanical remains show maize cultivation in a rural community during settlement of the semiarid northern Basin of Mexico. The economy was still changing and did not yet display identical dependence on every domesticated plant. One excavated village therefore corrects the atlas without standing in for its whole polygon.

At Alpuyeca in Morelos, INAH reconstructs spring-side villages around 1500 to 1200 BCE whose rain-fed milpa included maize, beans, and squash. Easy water access mattered even without irrigation. This is one local proposal tied to ceramics and settlement, not a universal recipe or proof that every family planted equal plots.

Maize-rich isotope values in eastern Maya lowlands coexist with local variation in forest plants, terrestrial animals, freshwater resources, age, mobility, and social access. Isotopes average foods over part of a life; they do not recover a Tuesday supper, name a cook, or turn everyone with similar carbon values into one culture.

Agricultural change unfolded over many generations. Regional evidence links improved multirow maize and standardized manos and metates with demographic transition, yet adoption varied in timing and intensity. A grinding stone demonstrates repeated work more securely than it demonstrates gender, household rank, language, or who got the first warm portion.

sections.title: Build villages from households, lakes, forests, and fields

items.text: Northern Honduran excavations place settled village life before 1600 BCE, sophisticated pottery by that date, and wider exchange by 1100 to 900 BCE. Those results challenge old center-and-periphery stories. People in the atlas’s southeastern reach were innovators and partners, not late students waiting for lessons from central Mexico.

Tlatilco residents farmed maize beside a lake rich in fish and birds. Mud-and-reed houses, hundreds of burials, pottery, and figurines reveal food, dwelling, adornment, and remembrance. The later Nahuatl place-name is not what residents called themselves, and a figurine’s hairstyle is evidence of representation, not a complete census.

Princeton’s securely dated Tlatilco figurines from about 1400 to 1100 BCE preserve modeled bodies, dress, gesture, and skilled clay work in miniature. They may reflect play, ritual, identity, teaching, or several purposes. Museum dates and materials are firm; the maker’s name, user’s age, and household jokes are not.

San Jose Mogote began occupation around 1500 BCE and grew into an Oaxacan regional center with public and private spaces and specialized production. This history includes farmers, craftspeople, leaders, and households in changing relationships. Its political prominence cannot be stretched across Central America merely because the atlas gives neighbors the same color.

Lowland Maya origins remain difficult because permanent houses and later construction disturbed earlier deposits. Controlled radiocarbon, subsistence, and technology evidence support dynamic local development, while pottery before about 1000 BCE remains uncertain. “No early pot found” is not “no people lived here,” and ceramics never carried passports.

sections.title: Make, trade, copy, and improve useful things

items.text: Cacao residues in Puerto Escondido vessels show drinks by at least 1100 BCE, probably first using fermented sweet pulp. Vessel shapes and neighboring styles reveal connections with El Salvador, Guatemala, and Mexico. Chemistry detects compounds, not a universal chocolate recipe, price, drinking age, or guarantee that every gathering served it.

Altica and Coapexco research traces obsidian from geological sources through processing and household exchange. Early toolkits often favored expedient flakes before pressure blades became widespread. A shiny edge may travel through gifts, barter, visiting kin, specialists, or middlemen; geochemistry finds the quarry, not the conversation at handoff.

Prismatic blades circulated widely during Early and Middle Formative times, but prepared blade cores moved extensively only in the Late Formative. That distinction matters: receiving finished blades differs from sustaining trained core preparation and pressure-flaking. “Obsidian trade” covers changing skills, packages, and relationships, not one timeless market system.

At Ceibal, El Chayal obsidian dominated early Middle Preclassic use before San Martin Jilotepeque became the principal source later. Highland stone reached lowland households as useful cutting material. The changing source pattern demonstrates durable exchange and consumer choices without proving that traders, rulers, or ethnic groups controlled every step.

Chemical analysis in the northern Maya lowlands finds local pottery production by 900 to 700 BCE and through later Middle Preclassic phases. Similar colors and forms can conceal different clay recipes, while local pots can join shared styles. A broken bowl is frustrating at lunch and excellent three thousand years later.

sections.title: Gather in plazas and watch towns become cities

items.text: At Ceibal between about 1000 and 350 BCE, households placed caches in floors and construction fill while public rituals used intrusive plaza pits. Domestic and civic practices developed together without being identical. The evidence shows residents actively shaping community life, rather than passive farmers obeying a single institution from the start.

Monte Alban was founded around 500 BCE and grew into a Zapotec capital on a leveled hilltop with terraced slopes, monumental buildings, tombs, and nearby agriculture. Its emergence helps explain why the atlas begins carving out named Oaxacan space. The city’s achievement belongs to its communities, not the leftover umbrella around it.

Cuicuilco joined lakes, forest resources, fields, homes, ritual buildings, imported materials, and water works in the Basin of Mexico. Researchers continue revising its dates and layout. Later lava preserved and destroyed evidence unevenly, so the site cannot be reduced to a neat rival that vanished on schedule for Teotihuacan.

Teotihuacan’s rapid urban expansion belongs mainly near and after 100 BCE, the final edge of this card. Earlier Formative villages and routes prepared the valley, but the later metropolis should not be projected backward over the 200 BCE residual polygon. City growth gathered migrants and institutions rather than revealing one earlier “Maize farmer” nation.

Public architecture, reservoirs, craft specialization, burials, and unequal goods can indicate coordination and hierarchy, but they do not all measure the same thing. A large mound may join labor through persuasion, obligation, celebration, fear, faith, or combinations. Political life differed among Oaxacan valleys, Maya lowlands, central basins, coasts, and frontiers.

sections.title: Meet families, children, neighbors, and unequal households

items.text: Archaeologists recover houses, hearth areas, storage, tools, food waste, burials, and rebuilding episodes rather than ancient family trees. A residence may hold parents, children, grandparents, other kin, visitors, workers, or changing groups over time. Household is a useful unit of activity, but it is not automatically a modern nuclear family.

Tlatilco burials and figurines make age, bodies, adornment, and remembrance visible, but not equally. More than 340 recorded burials came from a site heavily damaged by modern development. Children certainly lived in farming villages; survival, excavation, and early collecting decide whose traces enter the museum more than anyone’s historical importance.

Figurines display elaborate hair, clothing, body shapes, poses, and occasional paired faces. They show that appearance and skilled image-making mattered, yet they are not candid snapshots. A tiny clay person may compress identity, story, ritual, humor, instruction, or aesthetics, and usually declines to label which box the artist intended.

Household labor included planting, weeding, harvesting, carrying water and fuel, grinding, cooking, childcare, building, repairing, making tools, and maintaining social ties. Specific task assignments changed by place and status. Reviewed evidence does not justify giving all fieldwork to men, all grinding to women, or every lesson to elders.

Diet and health could differ by age, sex, residence, ecology, and access to valued foods. Isotope and skeletal studies reveal patterns, not personal preferences or fair shares. Children learned tastes and skills inside unequal households, but there is no atlas-wide record of weaning age, inheritance rules, marriage customs, or bedtime.

sections.title: Learn skills while writing evidence stays stubbornly local

items.text: Written-language sample for both exact atlas windows: none is securely attributable to this umbrella. No original script, transliteration, and translation can honestly represent every community from western Mexico through Central America. The safe result is explicit absence, not a later Maya quotation, modern Indigenous sentence, or borrowed sign presented as everyone’s speech.

San Andres objects near La Venta carry proposed Olmec writing around 650 BCE, but the atlas maps Olmec separately from “Maize farmers.” They belong to one specific Gulf Coast political setting and the signs are not a readable language sample for the target polygon. Adjacency is context, not permission to borrow.

San Jose Mogote Monument 3 has glyphs conventionally read as a calendrical name, often “1 Earthquake,” but specialists dispute whether its placement dates near 600 BCE or substantially later. Because date and reading are not secure enough for both exact windows, this card treats it as evidence about debate, not its sample.

A San Bartolo fragment securely preserves the Maya day sign “7 Deer” between 300 and 200 BCE. That is a wonderful small sample from a specific Maya community, but it falls inside the atlas’s 323 to 200 BCE gap, not either target window. The date makes the editorial silence measurable.

Children and novices could learn planting, weather reading, toolmaking, pottery, food preparation, ritual, and exchange by watching, helping, practicing, and being corrected. Local ceramic recipes and changing blade technologies imply transmitted skill. No reviewed exact-period source supplies a universal school, enrollment age, alphabet lesson, or standardized curriculum.

sections.title: Eat, drink, grind, fish, and plan for hungry seasons

items.text: Maize was increasingly important, but meals could also include beans, squash, chili, manioc, fruits, hunted animals, fish, mollusks, and locally available wild plants. Crop lists differ by soil, rainfall, elevation, and date. Calling every meal “corn” would be like calling an entire kitchen “the flour shelf.”

Grinding maize with a mano and metate required repetitive time and strength before cooking even began. Standardized equipment marks changing food production, yet tool wear cannot name the worker. The ancient kitchen offered no gym membership, but it could supply an impressive upper-body routine before breakfast.

Pottery expanded options for boiling, soaking, serving, storing, fermenting, and carrying foods and liquids. At Cuello, a long sequence from about 1200 BCE preserves changing ceramic spheres. Vessel style can date layers and trace connections, but soot, residue, shape, breakage, and context must support claims about actual use.

Cacao vessels show that some communities turned fruit or seeds into valued drinks, possibly for gatherings. Chemical residue proves presence more strongly than recipe or occasion. A beautiful bottle may have served hospitality, ritual, prestige, or ordinary refreshment; without a menu, “ancient hot chocolate party” remains a charming overconfident caption.

At Preclassic Kaminaljuyu and other sites, canals, shallow lakes, fields, gardens, fish, turtles, mollusks, and waterfowl could form integrated waterscapes. Farming was not isolated from fishing or gathering. Managing water also meant mud, mosquitoes, repairs, seasonal uncertainty, and many hands doing work that grand monuments rarely name.

sections.title: Handle health, water, waste, and the toilet question honestly

items.text: A skeletal comparison in Oaxaca grouped 1400 to 500 BCE communities with nonintensive agriculture and later communities with intensification. It found no simple overall health decline from intensification. Pooled skeletons can track stress and disease patterns, but preservation, age structure, sampling, and social difference prevent an atlas-wide medical score.

Carbon, nitrogen, sulfur, and oxygen isotopes help reconstruct averaged diet and movement, while bones and teeth can record injury, infection, workload, growth stress, and dental disease. None identifies every illness or cure. Surviving a healed injury may suggest care, but it rarely names the caregiver, medicine, prayer, or payment.

People treated pain, wounds, childbirth, fever, bites, and stomach trouble, but no secure target-wide medical manual or pharmacy survives. Plants could be food, medicine, craft material, ritual substance, or several at once. This card does not invent a universal healer class, dosage, surgery, or herbal cure from later practice.

Water systems were locally impressive. Maya communities built reservoirs and catchments after about 800 BCE; Tehuacan-Cuicatlan preserves dams, canals, wells, terraces, and aqueducts with different dates and jobs. Those works supported drinking, farming, and settlement, but a reservoir is not automatically clean water, equal access, or a sewer.

Toilet report: no reviewed source securely identifies one latrine type, sewer network, or waste rule shared across either polygon. People still managed excrement, ash, food scraps, broken pots, and animal waste through local practices. Archaeologists cannot promote every pit to “municipal sanitation” simply because the alternative smells historically inconvenient.

sections.title: Credit achievements and refuse two false endings

items.text: The deepest achievement was cumulative plant knowledge: selecting seed, matching crops to soils and rainfall, timing work, storing food, and combining fields with forests, lakes, rivers, hunting, and exchange. Maize agriculture was made by generations of Indigenous experimenters. It was never the achievement of an atlas category or one royal inventor.

Reservoirs, canals, terraces, dams, catchments, and drainage transformed difficult landscapes through observation and coordinated labor. At Cerros, builders shaped quarrying and settlement drainage; elsewhere, water storage sustained dry seasons. These systems were neither identical nor universally controlled by elites, and none makes the whole colored zone one hydraulic civilization.

Obsidian tools, local pottery, cacao vessels, figurines, monuments, and imported materials reveal technical experimentation and far-reaching relationships. Makers copied, translated, rejected, and improved styles rather than merely receiving influence from a single center. Similar-looking objects can celebrate connection while chemical composition quietly insists that local hands made them.

Writing and calendrical notation emerged in several specific settings, including Olmec, Oaxacan, and Maya communities, with dates and readings still debated. Their achievement deserves precision. Assigning every sign to generic “Maize farmers” would erase the very communities whose specialists carved, painted, read, displayed, and argued through those symbols.

Neither endpoint is a fall. At 323 BCE the atlas replaces two target pieces with other broad and named categories; after a gap it restores a smaller label for one century, then removes it at 100 BCE. Farmers, families, towns, crops, languages, and routes continue. The software changes color; history keeps moving.

ending.text: Neither target has a documented founding or fall. The first “Maize farmers” layer begins at 1500 BCE as the atlas retires a still larger umbrella, then persists through four identical broad polygons before splitting into two same-id features at 400 BCE. Both vanish at 323 BCE while named regions and local communities continue. The second id returns only for 200 to 100 BCE as a smaller residual polygon around separately mapped Teotihuacan, Monte Alban, and Maya areas. Its removal at 100 BCE does not end maize cultivation, villages, cities, languages, families, or exchange. The intervening 123-year gap even contains a securely dated Maya calendar sign, proving that evidence and atlas labels follow different clocks. Both overrides therefore keep fell null and successor lists empty. Continuity belongs to many distinct communities whose crops, skills, institutions, and descendants developed along separate paths, not to one imaginary maize-farmer nation.
